transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-17 15:00 UTC - Duration approx 45m - Attendees: Maya, Diego, JP (Redwood); Lena, Markus, Rachel, Tom (Seabreeze)

Summary (auto): Quick sync on pilot latency numbers. Discussed enabling streaming to reduce TTFT, tuning kernel choices for 8-bit quantized model, and gathering sequence-length histogram. Action items assigned.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): All right, hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate the time. We'll keep to 45 minutes. Quick roll call?
00:07 Speaker 2 (Lena): Hi, Lena here.
00:09 Speaker 3 (Markus): Markus on from infra.
00:11 Speaker 4 (Rachel): Rachel from security.
00:12 Speaker 1 (Maya): Great, Diego and JP from our side too. Diego is going to walk through the latency runs we did since last week. Diego?
00:20 Speaker 5 (Diego): Cool thanks. So we re-ran the TTFT profile with streaming enabled and disabled, and we tested three sequence buckets: short (1-32 tokens), medium (33-128), long (129-512). Overall headline: streaming shaves a fair bit off TTFT for short and medium, less so for long sequences where compute dominates.
00:45 Speaker 5 (Diego): For short seqs with streaming on we saw median TTFT drop from ~85ms to ~38ms on our dedicated A100-like nodes, p95 was 120ms -> 65ms. Non-streaming median stayed ~85ms. Note these numbers are on our internal perf cluster with kernel v2.4.
01:15 Speaker 6 (JP): I should call out that kernel v2.4 uses the new attention kernel that optimizes for 1-64 context, so we expected the short sequence gain. For 256+ we fall back to the generic kernel which is less optimized.
01:35 Speaker 3 (Markus): Quick q: when you say streaming are you talking about full chunked token streaming or the half-stream mode? Our app does chunk size 4.
01:43 Speaker 5 (Diego): We're testing true token streaming with 1-token flush; chunk size 1 effectively. We can try chunk=4 to match your production pattern, that should slightly increase TTFT but reduce CPU overhead.
02:02 Speaker 2 (Lena): Do you have numbers for chunk=4? That's what our integration uses.
02:07 Speaker 5 (Diego): Not yet, we'll run chunk=1 and chunk=4 in the next benchmark set. That's in the action items.
02:18 Speaker 4 (Rachel): From security, streaming is fine as long as we maintain in-flight encryption and KMS usage; any streaming buffer persisted on disk?
02:29 Speaker 5 (Diego): No disk persistence for streaming KV; it's in-memory KV cache. But worth noting we had a bug earlier where logs included partial responses - fixed now. We'll share the patch notes.
02:45 Speaker 1 (Maya): On the kernel/quantization front I dug into the notes with the perf team - the 8-bit quantized variant we deployed has two kernel paths: the quant-optimized attention kernel (fast for short seqs) and the fallback generic kernel. If Seabreeze's sequence distribution is mostly <128, we should pin that kernel path and adjust our compilation flags.
03:12 Speaker 2 (Lena): Our production distribution is actually bimodal - chat agents with short prompts ~20 tokens and batch reconciliation jobs that hit 300+ tokens occasionally. Markus, I think you have the histogram?
03:22 Speaker 3 (Markus): Yeah I'll export the histogram and share - roughly 60% under 64, 30% 64-256, 10% >256. We can send CSV.
03:33 Speaker 1 (Maya): Perfect, that's helpful. So tactical recommendation: enable streaming for the front-line chat flows, keep non-streaming for batch long-run jobs, and route by policy. We can set a model-route rule in the POC so short chat calls go to streaming-enabled pool with kernel v2.4 patched for quant, long jobs to a separate pool.
03:58 Speaker 6 (JP): Also consider prefix/KV caching - if many chat sessions reuse prompts, that's a big win for latency.
04:06 Speaker 2 (Lena): We already have a session cache on our side, but prefix reuse is limited.
04:11 Speaker 5 (Diego): Another point: TTFT includes network + cold kernel init. We noticed a small number of cold starts when model swapped kernels; warmup can help. We'll document warmup RPC and pre-warm strategies.
04:30 Speaker 3 (Markus): On infra config, our concern is autoscale latency during spikes - how quickly can Redwood Dedicated burst more workers?
04:37 Speaker 6 (JP): For Dedicated we support burst pools; configured autoscale can add pods in ~30-90s depending on image pull and node availability. For strict p99 SLOs we recommend reserved baseline capacity.
04:52 Speaker 4 (Rachel): Security question: For Dedicated or Private, we have to ensure KMS integration (HSM) is supported and audit logs for every inference call. Does Redwood provide per-token audit traces?
05:03 Speaker 1 (Maya): We provide structured tracing, and we can surface per-request metadata in audit logs. HSM/KMS integrations are supported in Private and Dedicated. We'll get the security pack doc over.
05:13 Speaker 2 (Lena): Great. Back to kernels - you mentioned a kernel v2.4. Is that public or experimental? We're worried about stability.
05:22 Speaker 5 (Diego): It's behind an opt-in flag in the POC; we've run it across a few customers with similar workloads, stability has been fine but we'll include a rollback path. We'll mark it experimental in the notes.
05:35 Speaker 1 (Maya): Ok quick demo of the benchmark dashboard - screen share omitted in this transcript - but notes: sample sizes 1k requests per bucket, run at QPS 40, concurrency 8, measured median/p95/p99 for TTFT and tail token latencies.
06:02 Speaker 5 (Diego): One interesting find: quantization to 8-bit saved ~35% CPU and helped throughput, but for some long prefix cases it slightly increased p99 due to extra dequant ops on the long kernel path. There's a tradeoff - we can selectively disable quant for long-jobs route.
06:30 Speaker 2 (Lena): That aligns with our expectations - cost vs worst-case tail latency tradeoff. We'll probably accept higher median improvements but need a p99 guardrail for our SLA.
06:47 Speaker 3 (Markus): For routing: can we do policy based on estimated sequence length prior to inference? We often can predict from request metadata.
06:56 Speaker 6 (JP): Yes, you can set routing by max_input_tokens or by a header. We'll show the routing rule example in the config.
07:10 Speaker 4 (Rachel): Another security note - data residency: some of our data cannot leave EU. Any regions support?
07:17 Speaker 1 (Maya): We have EU regions and can set model pools to EU-only. For Dedicated we can deploy inside customer VPC or private deployment if needed.
07:26 Speaker 2 (Lena): Cool. Back to streaming: do you support chunked streaming with backpressure? We saw a few reconnects in earlier test.
07:35 Speaker 5 (Diego): Yes we support backpressure and reconnect token replay; reconnects we've observed were network in the POC testbed but we'll instrument more metrics and surface them.
07:50 Speaker 1 (Maya): Let's capture the agreed benchmark matrix: seq buckets (1-32, 33-128, 129-512), streaming modes (off, chunk=1, chunk=4), kernel variant (v2.3 baseline, v2.4 quant-optimized), quant on/off. Diego to run with 1k samples each and provide CSVs.
08:12 Speaker 2 (Lena): For long-run batch jobs we will also test running on a pinned non-quantized kernel to measure p99.
08:20 Speaker 5 (Diego): Yep we'll include that comparison.
08:24 Speaker 3 (Markus): Regarding autoscale: can you provide expected throughput per-GPU for the quant vs non-quant variants? That helps us size nodes.
08:33 Speaker 6 (JP): We'll include throughput curves; quant tends to increase throughput ~1.4x on our hardware for these models but varies by seq len.
08:45 Speaker 1 (Maya): Any blockers from Seabreeze side?
08:48 Speaker 2 (Lena): Main blocker is we need the kernel notes and config change to review with compliance before toggling in prod. Also want the CSV histogram for sequences.
08:58 Speaker 3 (Markus): We'll export seq histogram and share by tomorrow.
09:02 Speaker 4 (Rachel): Security will review KMS/HSM doc once you share. Also please include the audit log example.
09:10 Speaker 1 (Maya): We'll upload the security pack and audit-sample.
09:14 Speaker 2 (Lena): Great. A small nit: in last week's run we saw a few transcripts with odd tokens like 'KV cash' in logs - is that noise in ASR or kernel naming?
09:26 Speaker 5 (Diego): That's likely transcription noise and our internal naming mismatch; we'll clean up log keys.
09:33 Speaker 1 (Maya): Ok, sprinting through wrap up. Recap: Diego runs the full benchmark matrix, Maya sends kernel/quant notes + rollback instructions and security docs, Markus and Lena provide seq histogram and SLA numbers. Plan infra deep-dive on 24th.
09:55 Speaker 2 (Lena): Sounds good.
09:58 Speaker 4 (Rachel): Thanks all.
10:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and update the POC board.
